WA:
The best part of Washington is that you can wake up to two different states. On the west side, the Olympic rainforest drips moss over the campgrounds and the Cascadia Marine Trail strings small camps along Puget Sound for anyone arriving by kayak. Drive over the Cascades and by afternoon you're in dry pine country, with the Methow Valley around Winthrop and the river camps up from Leavenworth.

Port Angeles is the easy base for the Olympics, and Marblemount puts you at the edge of the North Cascades. Some of the camps below are hike-in only, so read the details before you count on parking. The North Cascades Highway closes for snow, usually from November into spring.
TX:
Keep driving west in Texas and the state starts to feel empty in the best way. Past the Pecos the towns thin out, the sky gets bigger, and at Study Butte you're at the door of Big Bend, where the Chisos Mountains hold the last light after the desert floor has gone dark. It's a Dark Sky Park, and on a clear night it shows.

The campsites out there are backcountry, so get a park permit and give yourself time to reach them. Closer in, Bandera still calls itself the Cowboy Capital of the World, and Port Aransas lets you camp on the beach and fall asleep to the Gulf. Odessa and Midland, out in oil country, have a big cluster of RV parks, but a lot of the spaces go to oilfield crews, so call ahead.
OR:
There's a spot near Camp Sherman where the Metolius River comes up out of the ground at the foot of Black Butte, already a full river, cold and clear. The campgrounds downstream sit right on the bank, and it's hard to leave.

That's the Oregon Cascades in short: water everywhere. East of Glide, the North Umpqua runs green over the rocks past Toketee Falls, and up top, Crescent Lake and Lemolo are the kind of lakes you swim in once and remember. Oakridge and La Pine make good supply stops. The high campgrounds open late and close early for snow, so plan around summer and early fall.
MN:
Up on Rainy Lake near Ranier, the best sound of the night is the loons. A lot of the camps up there are on islands and shorelines you reach by boat, so if you're in a van, base yourself in Ranier or Orr and rent a boat for the day.

The North Shore is the other reason to come. From Grand Marais and Lutsen, Lake Superior looks more like an ocean than a lake, and the Superior National Forest campgrounds inland sit on quiet lakes with canoe launches. Around Cass Lake, the Chippewa National Forest has a few more. Summer is short and the bugs know it, so June through September is the window.
CO:
Drive Trail Ridge Road between Estes Park and Grand Lake and you'll cross the Continental Divide on the highest paved through-road in the country, with tundra on both sides. Those two towns frame Rocky Mountain National Park, and in September the elk gather in Moraine Park and bugle at dusk, right by the campground.

Estes Park has the park's drive-in campgrounds. The Grand Lake side is mostly hike-in sites that need a permit. Further afield, Red Feather Lakes, Gunnison and Bayfield have Forest Service campgrounds, and out by Dinosaur the camps are on the Green and Yampa rivers, for float trips. Many high campgrounds don't open until June.
MI:
Michigan's Upper Peninsula is where the state saves its best. At Pictured Rocks near Munising, sandstone cliffs streaked with copper and green drop straight into Lake Superior, and the water is clear enough to see the rocks far below. Grand Marais, further east, has small state forest campgrounds on quiet lakes, some with only a handful of sites.

Crossing the Mackinac Bridge into St. Ignace is half the fun of getting there. Below the bridge, Baldwin and Mio sit in the Huron-Manistee National Forest, with rivers made for a slow paddle. June brings the bugs and July brings the crowds, so late summer is the sweet spot.
UT:
Highway 128 out of Moab follows the Colorado River between red cliffs, and the small campgrounds along it put you right at the water with the Fisher Towers up the road. It's one of the prettiest drives in the West, and you can stop for the night.

If Moab feels busy, head for the San Rafael Swell around Temple Mountain, or up into the Henry Mountains outside Hanksville, said to be the last range mapped in the lower 48. Springdale is the gateway to Zion, and Flaming Gorge in the northeast has cool campgrounds above a red-rock reservoir. Desert summers are hot, so go high in July and August.
AK:
The best nights in Alaska might be in a Forest Service cabin in the Tongass. Woodstove, rain on the roof, a lake or a cove to yourself, and a floatplane or boat to get you there. Around Petersburg, Sitka and Wrangell there are dozens of them, and you reserve them ahead.

If you're on the road, the Kenai is the place. Cooper Landing sits on the bright turquoise Kenai River, Seward backs onto the fjords, and Whittier is a tunnel away on Prince William Sound. Near Paxson, the camps are for river trips rather than vehicles. Distances are long and services are thin, so fill up whenever you can.
WY:
Yellowstone is a different park after the day visitors leave. Most of the camps near West Yellowstone, Silver Gate and Mammoth are backcountry sites, where you might share a meadow with bison and hear a geyser go off in the dark. The Bechler corner near Warm River is called Cascade Corner for its waterfalls.

On the Grand Teton side, the camps near Kelly look straight up at the range. All of these need a backcountry permit, and you walk or paddle in. For drive-in camping, the gateway towns and Cody have private parks. Road campgrounds in both parks book up months ahead, and the high country holds snow into June.
PA:
Michaux State Forest near Fayetteville sits near the Appalachian Trail's halfway point, and the thru-hikers passing through Pine Grove Furnace are good company. The forest has simple numbered campsites in the trees, and Gettysburg is a short drive away.

In the northwest, Marienville sits in the Allegheny National Forest, which turns red and gold in October. Lancaster County, around Conestoga, is farm country, with roadside stands and the clip of buggies on the back roads. Most listings here are private campgrounds, so check their seasons before you go.
FL:
The most Florida way to spend a night is on a chickee in the Everglades: a raised wooden platform with a roof, built over the water where there's no dry land to camp on. Out of Chokoloskee and the Flamingo side near Florida City, the backcountry sites are strung along the Wilderness Waterway, and you get to them by canoe or kayak with a permit. The stars over the mangroves are worth the paddle.

If you're driving, the Keys are the other draw. Islamorada, Duck Key and Marathon have RV parks right on the water, and they fill up fast in winter. Go between December and April. Summer brings heat, storms and mosquitoes that will change your plans for you.
NC:
Drive into Cataloochee Valley above Maggie Valley around dusk and you'll likely find elk grazing in the old fields, a short way from the road. They were brought back to the Smokies in 2001, and this quiet corner of the park is where they settled.

Most of North Carolina's listings are backcountry sites in Great Smoky Mountains National Park, the numbered ones near Bryson City, Cherokee and Cosby. You need a park reservation and you hike in. Across Fontana Lake from Fontana Dam, a few of them are easiest to reach by boat. Up in the High Country near Seven Devils and Boone, there are drive-in campgrounds and cooler nights when the lowlands are sticky.
MT:
Montana lets you rent an old fire lookout for the night. Garver Mountain near Yaak and Webb Mountain above Lake Koocanusa near Rexford are two of them: a room on stilts with windows on every side and the whole valley below. Forest Service cabins near Sula, Neihart and Augusta work the same way. Book ahead, bring your own water, and expect a gravel road at the end.

For drive-in campgrounds, Red Lodge sits at the foot of the Beartooth Highway, and Augusta is where the plains run into the Rocky Mountain Front. Canyon Ferry near York has campgrounds along the reservoir outside Helena. High roads and campgrounds often stay snowed in until June.
TN:
Townsend calls itself the peaceful side of the Smokies, and it earns it. It's the back door to Cades Cove, where deer graze around old log cabins and churches at first light. Get there early, before the loop road fills with cars.

Most of Tennessee's listings are numbered backcountry sites in Great Smoky Mountains National Park, around Townsend, Gatlinburg and Cosby. You need a park reservation and you hike in. If you want hookups instead, Pigeon Forge is lined with RV resorts. For something quieter, the Cherokee National Forest campgrounds near Coker Creek sit along mountain streams, and Spring City has lakeside parks on Watts Bar Lake.
ID:
Stanley is a tiny town with the Sawtooth Mountains standing right behind it, sharp and close enough that they look painted on. On a calm morning at Redfish Lake just south of town, the peaks show up twice, once in the sky and once in the water. Stanley has the biggest cluster of campgrounds in the state, and it's often one of the coldest places in the country overnight, even in summer.

Beyond Stanley, Lowman sits on the Payette River with hot springs along the road, and Idaho City is an old gold-rush town with Forest Service cabins in the hills around it. In the east, Island Park has campgrounds along the Henry's Fork near Yellowstone. Up north, Elk City is about as remote as Idaho gets, so fill up before you go.
WI:
Paddle out from the mainland near Bayfield on a calm day and you can slip into the sea caves of the Apostle Islands, where Lake Superior has hollowed the red sandstone into arches and rooms. Little Sand Bay is the easy campground on shore, and a few island sites are reachable only by boat.

The rest of Wisconsin's best camping is in the Northwoods. Around Sayner and Eagle River, the state forest campgrounds sit on one lake after another, Plum, Starrett, Razorback, with loons on most of them. Further south and west, the Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest has quiet campgrounds near Mellen and Long Lake. Summer is short and busy, and September is often the better month.
GA:
Amicalola Falls drops more than 700 feet down a mountainside near Dawsonville, the tallest waterfall in Georgia, and the trail from the top is the traditional start of the walk to Springer Mountain and the Appalachian Trail. If you stay nearby, you'll meet hikers on their first night out.

The north Georgia mountains around Blairsville, Helen and Morganton are full of Chattahoochee National Forest campgrounds, at places like Lake Winfield Scott, DeSoto Falls and along the Toccoa River. On the coast, St. Marys is where the ferry leaves for Cumberland Island, with wild horses on the beach and camping by permit. Around Hartwell, the Corps of Engineers campgrounds line the lake.
MO:
The springs are the thing in Missouri. Around Eminence, cold clear water comes up out of the ground and feeds the Current and Jacks Fork rivers, and at Alley Spring an old red mill still sits over the pool. The campgrounds at Alley Spring, Round Spring and Two Rivers put you right on the water for a float the next morning.

About 65 of the state's listings are agency campgrounds, many of them Corps of Engineers parks on lakes like Clearwater near Piedmont, Wappapello near Puxico and Mark Twain Lake near Center. Branson has the most private RV parks if you want shows and hookups. Bennett Spring draws trout fishers from opening day in March.
NV:
Valley of Fire, near Moapa Valley, is red sandstone that glows at sunset, and the campgrounds at Atlatl Rock and Arch Rock sit right among it. Atlatl Rock is named for the petroglyphs on its face, carved long before anyone drove out here.

When Las Vegas is baking, Mount Charleston is the escape, with Forest Service campgrounds in the pines an hour from the Strip and much cooler air. In the northeast, Angel Lake above Wells is a high alpine lake at the end of a steep road. Kingston, in the Toiyabe Range off Highway 50, has small campgrounds along the creek. Las Vegas, Reno and Pahrump have most of the RV parks.
AL:
Alabama's most unusual camping is in the Mobile-Tensaw Delta near Stockton, where the Bartram Canoe Trail has wooden platforms built over the water. You paddle in, tie up and sleep surrounded by swamp and cypress, with nothing but the frogs for company. Book a platform and bring a good bug net.

Most of the state's listings are down on the Gulf Coast. Foley, Gulf Shores and the towns around Bon Secour and Magnolia Springs have a long run of RV resorts, and Gulf State Park has a big campground a short walk from the beach. Winter is high season here, when snowbirds come south, and spring and fall are the most comfortable.
OK:
Beavers Bend, outside Hochatown in the far southeast corner, doesn't look like the Oklahoma most people picture. Tall pines crowd the Mountain Fork River, the water runs cold below Broken Bow Dam, and people fish for trout there all year. The park's campgrounds, Dogwood, Elm, Grapevine, sit right in the trees.

Out west, Granite puts you near the granite domes of Quartz Mountain, and Black Kettle National Grassland near Strong City is wide-open prairie. Sulphur is the base for the Chickasaw National Recreation Area, with campgrounds by springs and swimming holes. Fort Cobb and the lakes near Norman and Kaw City round out the list.
OH:
Loudonville calls itself the Canoe Capital of Ohio, and on a summer weekend the Mohican River proves it. The campgrounds there rent boats and run shuttles upriver, so you can float back to your site, and Mohican State Park has its own campground in the hemlocks along the gorge.

In the southwest, Caesar Creek near Harveysburg is one of the few places you can legally take home fossils, with a free permit from the visitor center. Up on Lake Erie, Oak Harbor sits by the marshes where birders gather every May for the spring warbler migration. Seneca Lake near Senecaville has campgrounds and RV parks around the water.
VA:
Virginia has wild ponies in two places, and you can camp near both. On the coast, Chincoteague is the gateway to Assateague, where the ponies graze the marsh and walk the beach. In the far southwest, the campgrounds near Troutdale, Grindstone and Hurricane among them, sit below Grayson Highlands, where a different herd wanders the open balds near Mount Rogers.

In between, Front Royal is the north end of Skyline Drive and Shenandoah National Park. The Forest Service campgrounds around Hot Springs ring Lake Moomaw in the George Washington National Forest. Virginia Beach has First Landing State Park and a cluster of RV parks near the ocean, and Philpott Lake near Bassett has quiet Corps campgrounds.
IL:
Southern Illinois is the surprise. Cave-In-Rock, on the Ohio River, is a cave in the bluff that river pirates once used as a hideout, and the state park above it has camping. A short drive north, Camp Cadiz sits in the Shawnee National Forest near Garden of the Gods, where sandstone formations look out over miles of forest.

Further north, Carlyle Lake is the biggest man-made lake in the state, with Corps campgrounds along the dam, and Lake Shelbyville has more around Lithia Springs and Lone Point. Up near the Wisconsin line, the Chain O'Lakes campgrounds near Fox Lake are good for paddling. Kinkaid Lake near Harrison is a quiet spot in the south.
NY:
On Lake George, near Bolton Landing, the state runs campsites on the islands themselves. You reach them by boat, and you get a small island, a fire ring and the lake to yourself once the day boats head home. Fork Island and Little Harbor Island are among the ones listed.

The Adirondacks hold most of the rest. Around Speculator, small campsites sit on remote lakes like the Cedar Lakes. Near Lake Placid, Lake Colden is a backcountry camp in the High Peaks, and Wilmington Notch has a drive-in campground under Whiteface. Port Henry has campgrounds on Lake Champlain, and out west, Westfield sits in grape country on Lake Erie.
AR:
Near Murfreesboro, Crater of Diamonds is the one place in the world where the public can dig for diamonds in their original volcanic source and keep whatever they find. People turn up stones every year, and the state park has a campground a short walk from the field.

The Ozarks hold most of the rest. Blanchard Springs near Fifty-Six has campgrounds by a cold spring below the caverns, and Mountain View is known for the music on its courthouse square. Beaver Lake near Lost Bridge Village, DeGray Lake near Bismarck and Greers Ferry near Heber Springs have Corps campgrounds on the water, and the Cossatot River near Wickes has some of the wildest rapids in the state.
WV:
Spruce Knob, near Whitmer, is the highest point in West Virginia, and on a clear night the sky up there is about as dark as it gets in the East. Spruce Knob Lake has a campground in the spruce, and Seneca Rocks, the sharp sandstone fin climbers come for, is just down the road.

Summersville Lake is the other standout, with water clear enough that people scuba dive in it and cliffs along the shore. Canaan Valley near Harman sits high and cool, and the Cranberry River near Richwood runs through the Monongahela National Forest. Burnsville and Flatwoods have Corps campgrounds in the middle of the state, handy off I-79.
IN:
Brown County in October is the reason to camp in Indiana. The hills around Nashville turn red and gold, the little town fills with galleries and fudge shops, and the campgrounds outside it book up for every fall weekend. Get in early or come midweek.

Near Spencer, McCormick's Creek was Indiana's first state park, with a canyon and a waterfall a short walk from camp. Shades State Park near Alamo has backpack and canoe camps above Sugar Creek, and Hardin Ridge in the Hoosier National Forest sits on Lake Monroe. Most of the rest of the listings are private campgrounds and RV parks.
SC:
Up in the far northwest corner near Tamassee, the Chattooga River runs wild and protected through the Sumter National Forest, and Cherry Hill Campground sits in the cool woods nearby. It's a different state from the beaches, quieter and greener, with waterfalls a short hike from the road.

Most of South Carolina's listings are RV parks, and they follow the coast and the interstates. Myrtle Beach has big campgrounds near the sand, Hilton Head has a motorcoach resort for big rigs, and Lake Greenwood near Cross Hill has lakeside parks. Around Greenville and Spartanburg, RV parks near Taylors and Duncan are easy stops off I-85.
NH:
Drive the Kancamagus Highway from Lincoln toward Bartlett in early October and the White Mountains are on fire with color. The Forest Service campgrounds along it, Jigger Johnson, Blackberry Crossing and Covered Bridge among them, sit right by the Swift River, where people swim on warm days.

A lot of New Hampshire's listings are backcountry tentsites in the White Mountains. Near Lincoln, Liberty Spring sits on the Appalachian Trail below Franconia Ridge, and Thirteen Falls is deep in the Pemigewasset Wilderness. Near Gorham, the Valley Way climbs toward the Presidentials. Bethlehem and Twin Mountain have drive-in campgrounds if you'd rather sleep near the car.
KY:
Under the hills around Brownsville runs Mammoth Cave, the longest known cave system in the world, and you can camp right on top of it. Maple Springs is the drive-in campground, and the backcountry sites like Sal Hollow and Raymer Hollow are a hike into the woods above the caves.

In the east, Red River Gorge near Campton is full of sandstone arches, and the climbers who come for its cliffs end the day with pizza in town. Cave Run Lake near Farmers has Forest Service campgrounds at Zilpo and Twin Knobs. Down south near Corbin, Cumberland Falls is one of the few places you can see a moonbow on a clear night with a full moon. Land Between the Lakes near Cadiz covers the west.
ND:
The badlands around Medora come as a shock after hours of flat prairie. In Theodore Roosevelt National Park, bison wander the road, prairie dog towns cover the flats, and a band of wild horses lives in the hills. The campgrounds around Medora put you right at the edge of it.

The park's quieter north unit is near Watford City, with campgrounds in the national grassland nearby. Lake Sakakawea, behind Garrison Dam near Pick City, is a huge reservoir with campgrounds and walleye fishing along the shore, and Lake Ashtabula near Sibley has Corps campgrounds in the east. Summers are short and winds are strong, so stake everything down.
AZ:
Drive up the Catalina Highway from Tucson and in about an hour you go from saguaro cactus to pine forest. The campgrounds on Mount Lemmon, Molino, Rose Canyon and Whitetail among them, can be thirty degrees cooler than the desert floor. Arizona is full of escapes like that.

The Mogollon Rim near Christopher Creek has campgrounds around Woods Canyon Lake at the top of a 2,000-foot cliff. In the White Mountains near Greer, the campgrounds at Big Lake are named for the trout people catch there. Oak Creek Canyon above Sedona has campgrounds by the creek under red rock walls, and Prescott has Lynx Lake. Most high campgrounds close for winter.
LA:
New Iberia is in the heart of Cajun country, and a stay there is mostly about the food: boudin from a gas station counter, crawfish in season, and Avery Island just down the road, where Tabasco has been made for more than 150 years. The RV parks around town make a good base for the bayous.

Most of Louisiana's listings are RV parks along I-10 and I-20. Lake Charles and the towns around it, Sulphur, Westlake and Moss Bluff, have the biggest cluster, near the casinos and the Gulf. Up north, Bossier City and Greenwood sit outside Shreveport. Summers are hot and wet, so spring and fall are the times to come.
MS:
The Natchez Trace Parkway runs 444 miles from Natchez to Nashville with no billboards, no trucks and a speed limit that makes you slow down. It follows an old path used for centuries, and Natchez State Park near the southern end is a good place to start.

Vicksburg, on the bluffs above the Mississippi, has the Civil War battlefield and a couple of RV parks near the river. In the north, Enid Lake near Pope and the Tennessee-Tombigbee Waterway near Columbus have Corps campgrounds on the water. Tunica's casinos run their own RV parks if you want hookups and a buffet. About 20 of the state's listings are agency campgrounds.
